stops.name: Allen's Landing
stops.description: The Allen brothers came ashore here in August 1836 and platted a city on the spot, making this bend where White Oak Bayou meets Buffalo Bayou the recognized birthplace of Houston.

stops.name: Market Square Park
stops.description: Houston set this block aside as a public square in 1836 and built four successive city halls on it, the last in 1904, before it became the shaded park at the center of the historic district.

stops.name: Houston Cotton Exchange Building
stops.description: Built in 1884 for the traders who set the price of Texas cotton, this brick exchange is a reminder that Houston was a commodity town long before it was an oil one.

stops.name: W. L. Foley Building
stops.description: This Travis Street merchant block dates to 1860 and has been rebuilt after fire twice, in 1889 and again in 1994, which makes it one of the most stubbornly persistent buildings downtown.

stops.name: Sweeney, Coombs, and Fredericks Building
stops.description: The three story corner turret and Eastlake trim here survive from 1889, when this was ordinary commercial architecture rather than one of the last Victorian buildings left downtown.

stops.name: Kiam Building
stops.description: Clothier Ed Kiam's 1893 Romanesque Revival store was the first building in Houston to run an electric elevator, and it was wired for electric light when most of the city was not.

stops.name: 1910 Harris County Courthouse
stops.description: This six story Classical Revival courthouse still hears cases as the seat of the First and Fourteenth Texas Courts of Appeals, and two of its courtrooms rise a full two stories inside.

stops.name: The Rice
stops.description: Three buildings have stood on this corner, the first of them the Capitol of the Republic of Texas, and the 1913 hotel that eventually replaced it now holds apartments.

stops.name: Christ Church Cathedral
stops.description: The congregation here was founded in 1839, when Texas was still an independent republic, and it is the oldest surviving congregation in the city.

stops.name: The Sam Houston Hotel
stops.description: Built in 1924 for business travelers on a budget, this narrow brick hotel sat closed from the 1970s until a full restoration brought it back as a boutique hotel.

stops.name: JPMorgan Chase Building
stops.description: Finished in 1929 as the Gulf Building, this Art Deco tower was the tallest thing in Houston for the next thirty four years and is still the city's best surviving prewar skyscraper.

stops.name: Esperson Buildings
stops.description: Mellie Esperson raised the 1927 tower as a memorial to her husband Niels and crowned it with a tempietto copied from Rome, giving downtown its only full Italian Renaissance building.

stops.name: Pennzoil Place
stops.description: Philip Johnson and John Burgee cut the tops of these twin bronze towers on a slant in 1976 and set them a few feet apart, so the slot between them changes shape as you walk the block.

stops.name: Alley Theatre
stops.description: The oldest professional theatre company in Texas has worked here since 1947, and its fortress like 1968 concrete home is as much a landmark as the company inside it.

stops.name: Houston City Hall
stops.description: Houston's 1939 seat of government is a limestone Art Deco slab set behind a reflecting pool, flanked by Tranquillity Park on one side and the public library on the other.

note: Houston had never been scouted; the rotation had run Atlanta through Green Bay. All 15 stops sit inside the downtown core and form a walkable loop of roughly 1.3 miles: Allen's Landing and Market Square at the north end, the Victorian Main and Travis Street blocks, the Texas Avenue hotels and cathedral, the Art Deco and modernist towers on Main and Milam, then west to the Theater District and City Hall. Every address comes from the downtown Houston NRHP listing or the stop's own article, never from coordinates. ZIP check worth knowing about: OpenStreetMap returned 77003 for the Rice and Christ Church and 77004 for the 1910 courthouse, which contradicted every neighboring address; the US Census geocoder resolved all fifteen to 77002 and that is what is filed here, so the OSM building tags appear to be wrong rather than the block sitting on a ZIP boundary. Dropped on purpose: the downtown skyscraper articles that are only tenant lists (Heritage Plaza, 1000 Main, Wells Fargo Plaza and similar), light rail stations, schools and hospitals, the Main Street Market Square Historic District itself as a district rather than a standable place, and Sam Houston Coliseum and Houston Music Hall, both demolished. Left out for distance rather than quality, all still good candidates for a second Houston run: Sam Houston Park with the Kellum-Noble House, the Julia Ideson Building, Jones Hall, Wortham Theater Center, Sesquicentennial Park, Tranquillity Park, Union Station at Daikin Park, the US Customhouse and the Humble Oil Building.
